sermon:
There is a kind of letter you only write to people you cannot reach. Peter writes from Rome to believers scattered across five Roman provinces in what is now Turkey — Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, Bithynia. He cannot visit them. He can only put hope in ink and trust it to a courier named Silvanus. And the first thing he calls them is not converts, not church members, but the strangest word in the letter: exiles. Elect exiles. Chosen, and displaced. Both at once.

That word is the whole letter in miniature. These were people who had lost standing. Some had lost family, some had lost trade, some had lost the protection a neighbor extends to someone who fits. They had become foreigners in the towns where they were born. And Peter does not begin by promising the towns will warm to them. He begins higher up than that.

**Born into an inheritance the fire cannot reach**

Listen to where he starts. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. According to his great mercy, he has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you" (1 Peter 1:3-4). Read that slowly, because it is built like a wall against panic. Imperishable — it cannot rot. Undefiled — it cannot be soiled. Unfading — it cannot lose its color. Three Greek words stacked against three ways every earthly inheritance dies. And then the line that holds them up: kept in heaven for you. Guarded. Reserved. Under a name that is yours.

This is why Peter calls the hope living. It is not wishful. It is not the hope that a thing might turn out. It is hope with a pulse, hope that came alive on the morning the tomb came up empty. The resurrection is not the decoration on Peter's gospel. It is the foundation under the exile's feet. You were not merely encouraged. You were born again — given a second birth into a family that cannot be foreclosed on.

**Trials that prove the gold is real**

Then Peter does something pastors are tempted to skip. He names the suffering directly. "In this you rejoice, though now for a little while, if necessary, you have been grieved by various trials" (1 Peter 1:6). Notice he does not pretend the grief is small. He calls it grief. But he sets a frame around it: for a little while, if necessary. The fire has a clock on it, and the fire has a purpose under it.

And the purpose is the most honest thing in the chapter. "So that the tested genuineness of your faith — more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire — may be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ" (1 Peter 1:7). Gold is refined by being held in the flame until the impurity rises and is skimmed off. Peter says faith works the same way. The fire does not come to destroy what you believe. It comes to prove it was ever yours. A faith that has only ever been comfortable has never been tested, and a faith that has never been tested does not yet know whether it is gold or only paint.

Let me be honest about where this lands, because I have failed it. When the trial comes I do not first reach for the inheritance kept in heaven. I reach for an explanation. I reach for someone to blame. I treat the fire as an insult rather than a refining. And Peter, who denied his Lord three times by a fire of his own, knows that man. He is writing to me as much as to them.

**Christ at the center of it**

Who holds this together. The prophets, Peter says, searched and inquired about this very salvation, "inquiring what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories" (1 Peter 1:11). There is the pattern stamped on the whole letter: the sufferings, and then the glory. Christ went into the fire first. He was refined in a furnace no one else could survive, and he came out the other side raised and crowned. The exile's path is not a detour around his cross. It is the road behind him. You do not love him yet you love him, you do not see him yet you believe — and you rejoice with a joy that is inexpressible and full of glory, because the One who walked through suffering into glory is bringing you the same way home.

The fire is real. So is the gold. And the gold does not burn.

Your hope outlasts the fire.

There is a word from the old world that we have lost, and Peter builds this passage on it. Ransom. In the first century it meant the price paid to buy a slave out of the market, or to buy a prisoner out of captivity. You did not earn your way out. Someone with money you did not have laid it down, and the chain came off. Peter writes to scattered believers and tells them their chain came off — but not for the price they would have guessed.

"Knowing that you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot" (1 Peter 1:18-19). Silver and gold buy most things. They could not buy this. The price was blood, and not the blood of an animal led to a temple, but the blood of the Lamb God had been pointing to since the first Passover. That is the foundation of everything Peter asks next. He never commands before he reminds. He tells you what you cost before he tells you how to live.

**Holiness is the response, not the price**

Watch the order, because the church inverts it constantly. We treat holiness as the toll booth before God's acceptance. Peter treats it as the answer to acceptance already given. "As obedient children, do not be conformed to the passions of your former ignorance, but as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, You shall be holy, for I am holy" (1 Peter 1:14-16). He is quoting Leviticus, lifting a command given to Israel and laying it on exiles in Asia Minor. The logic is family logic. Be holy because of whose you are. The Father is holy; the children carry the family likeness into a world that does not recognize it.

And holiness here is not retreat. Peter begins, "Preparing your minds for action, and being sober-minded, set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ" (1 Peter 1:13). The old translation pictured a man gathering up his long robe and tucking it into his belt so he could move. Holiness is not standing still in a clean room. It is a man dressed to work, with his hope fixed on the day Christ appears.

**Love that proves the new birth**

Then Peter turns the inward holiness outward, and he will not let it stay private. "Having purified your souls by your obedience to the truth for a sincere brotherly love, love one another earnestly from a pure heart" (1 Peter 1:22). The word he uses for earnestly means stretched out, strained, the way a muscle is pulled to its limit. Casual affection is not what he asks. He asks for love that costs something, love that keeps loving past the point where it would be reasonable to stop.

And he grounds it in the seed of the new birth itself. "You have been born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God" (1 Peter 1:23). The same Father, the same imperishable seed, the same living word — which means the believer next to you, the one who annoys you, the one who let you down, was planted from the same imperishable seed you were. You cannot honor the word and despise the person it gave birth to.

**The honest application**

So Peter lists what has to go. "Put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander" (1 Peter 2:1). Read that list slowly and you find it is not a list of scandals. It is a list of church sins. Malice — the grudge you keep warm. Deceit — the version of the story that flatters you. Hypocrisy — the face you put on for Sunday. Envy — the quiet ache when a brother is blessed. Slander — the thing you say when he is not in the room. I know that list because I have practiced every line of it, and I have done it while preaching holiness. The price was paid for me to be free of exactly these, and I keep reaching back into the market to pick them up again.

What does Peter put in their place. "Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation — if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good" (1 Peter 2:2-3). A newborn does not negotiate over the breast. It cries for it. Peter says: crave the word the way an infant craves milk, because you have tasted that the Lord is good — and a man who has tasted the goodness of the One who bled for him does not go back to the chains.

Bought at that price. Be holy.

Every builder knows the moment. A stone is hauled to the site, looked over, and set aside. Wrong shape, wrong grain, a flaw the master mason will not risk in his wall. It gets rolled to the edge of the lot and forgotten. Peter takes that ordinary scene and turns it into the center of his gospel. There was a stone the builders rejected. And God picked it up and made it the cornerstone.

"As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house" (1 Peter 2:4-5). Hold those two judgments side by side, because the whole passage lives in the gap between them. Rejected by men. Chosen by God. The same stone, two verdicts, and they do not agree. Peter writes to exiles who were rejected by men, and he tells them they are being built into the house God is raising on the very stone the world threw away.

**Rejected by men, chosen by God**

This is the key that unlocks the exile's confusion. You feel discarded by your town, your family, your trade — and you wonder if the verdict of men is the final word over your life. Peter says the cornerstone Himself was discarded. "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone" (1 Peter 2:7). The world's rejection of Christ did not lower his worth by a fraction. God's choice settled it, and the world's verdict was simply wrong. So when you are set aside, do not assume the men who set you aside saw clearly. They did not see clearly when the stone they handled was the Son of God.

And then Peter says the most dignifying thing in the letter. "But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light" (1 Peter 2:9). Every title there was once Israel's. Peter hands them to a band of scattered, slandered believers who own no temple and hold no power. You are not nobody. You are a priesthood. You are a holy nation. You are God's own possession. The world has the wrong file on you.

**The pattern that costs**

Then Peter turns and asks something hard. If you are this honored, how do you live among people who treat you as nothing. Not with rebellion. "Be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution" (1 Peter 2:13). Honor the emperor — and the emperor at the time was Nero. Servants, be subject to your masters, even the unjust ones. This is where the modern reader bristles, and Peter does not soften it. He raises the stakes. "For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly" (1 Peter 2:19).

Let me be honest where this presses on me. My instinct under unjust treatment is the cutting reply, the score kept, the small revenge dressed up as honesty. Peter knew that instinct in himself — he once drew a sword in a garden. And the man who drew the sword writes here that the way of the exile is not the sword. It is the wound absorbed without returning it.

**Following the steps of the Stone**

Because that is exactly what Christ did, and Peter will not let it stay abstract. "For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps. He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly" (1 Peter 2:21-23). There is the pattern stamped on the believer's life: when reviled, he did not revile back. He entrusted himself. He handed the verdict to the only Judge who sees clearly.

And Peter cannot leave the cross as mere example, because example alone saves no one. "He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed. For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls" (1 Peter 2:24-25). The Stone they rejected did not only show us how to suffer. He suffered to carry our sin. The example and the atonement are the same cross. You imitate him only because he first ransomed you.

Follow the Stone they rejected.

There is a kind of beauty that does not show up in a photograph. Peter names it in this chapter, and he names it precisely because the world he wrote into measured a woman by braided hair, gold jewelry, fine clothes — the visible markers of a household's standing. Peter does not ban any of it. He relocates the center of gravity. "Do not let your adorning be external — the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear — but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious" (1 Peter 3:3-4). The hidden person of the heart. The part no photograph catches and no jeweler can sell.

Peter writes this first to wives, some of them married to unbelieving husbands, in a culture where a wife was expected to take her husband's gods as her own. These women had not. They had a Lord their husbands did not share, and they could not preach him at the dinner table without making the house worse. So Peter gives them a quieter strategy: "so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives" (1 Peter 3:1). Won without a word. A life that argues when speech is closed off.

**The beauty the world cannot photograph**

Do not mistake gentle and quiet for weak and silent. The same word for gentle is used of Christ, who cleared a temple with a whip. This is strength under control, the power to retaliate held deliberately in check. It is the hardest courage there is — the courage to stay tender in a hard house. And Peter does not let the husbands off. "Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman... since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered" (1 Peter 3:7). Honor her as a fellow heir, he says, or your prayers hit the ceiling. God will not hear a man pray over a wife he dishonors.

**Suffering for doing good**

Then Peter widens the lens from the home to the hostile world, and the principle holds. "Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless" (1 Peter 3:9). This is the same instinct he named at the cross in the chapter before — the wound absorbed, not returned. And he is realistic about the cost: "But even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed" (1 Peter 3:14). Not if you suffer for being foolish. For being righteous. There is a suffering that comes simply from belonging to Christ in a world that does not, and Peter will not pretend it away.

Into that suffering comes the line this whole series leans on. "In your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:15). Notice the order. First, honor Christ as holy in your heart — settle the question of who is Lord inside, before the questioner ever shows up. Then be ready. And then the tone: gentleness and respect. Not the loud win. Not the clever takedown. A reason, given gently, by someone whose life has already raised the question.

Let me sit in my own failure here. I am quick with the defense and slow with the gentleness. I can give the reason and lose the respect in the same breath, and a defense delivered with contempt has already lost the argument it meant to win. The verse asks for a softer thing than I am naturally able to give.

**Christ, the righteous for the unrighteous**

Where does the strength for any of this come from. Peter points, as he always does, to the cross. "For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit" (1 Peter 3:18). There is the gospel in one line. The righteous, for the unrighteous. The innocent absorbed the wound the guilty had earned, and he did it to bring us to God — not merely to forgive us at a distance but to walk us into the room. Every quiet beauty, every blessing returned for cursing, every gentle answer, traces back to that exchange. You can suffer the righteous-for-unrighteous pattern only because Christ suffered it first and brought you home.

Suffer well. Answer with hope.

Peter reaches for a soldier's word. Arm yourselves. A man going into battle does not stroll out unarmed and hope the day goes well. He puts on what will keep him alive. Peter says the believer faces a fight too, and there is a weapon to take up, and it is a way of thinking. "Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin" (1 Peter 4:1). The weapon is Christ's own mind toward suffering — the settled resolve that there are things worth more than comfort, and that following him may cost the flesh, and that this is acceptable.

What does this mindset decide. It decides that the old life is over. "For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do" (1 Peter 4:3). Peter lists the old appetites — sensuality, drunkenness, the wild parties — and then names the real friction. The former friends are surprised. "With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you" (1 Peter 4:4). There is the exile's daily cost. Not a sword to the neck, but a circle that no longer makes sense to you, and is offended that it no longer does. The maligning starts there, at the party you left.

**Stewarding the grace you were given**

Then Peter turns the armed believer toward the body of Christ, and the tone shifts from defense to gift. "As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace" (1 Peter 4:10). A steward owns nothing. He manages what belongs to the master. Every ability you have for the church is on loan, and you will give an account of how you spent it. The varied grace — Peter pictures grace as multicolored, given in different forms to different people, so that no one carries the whole load and no one is left with nothing to give.

And it runs on love that covers. "Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins" (1 Peter 4:8). Covers — not exposes, not catalogs, not relitigates. A church of armed exiles cannot afford to keep a record of one another's failures. Love throws a cloak over the offense and keeps walking. Then the warmest line in the chapter, easy to miss: "Show hospitality to one another without grumbling" (1 Peter 4:9). Without grumbling. Peter knows we will open the door and resent the guest. He asks for the open door and the quiet heart together.

**Do not be surprised by the fire**

Then the warning that gives this sermon its weight. "Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you" (1 Peter 4:12). Surprise is the trap. We absorb a quiet theology that says a faithful life should be a protected life, and when the fire comes we feel cheated, as if a contract were broken. Peter says no contract was broken. The fire was always part of the road. "But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed" (1 Peter 4:13). Sufferings now, glory then — the same pattern from the first chapter, stamped on the exile's whole life.

Here is where I have to indict myself. I have preached this and then felt personally insulted by the very trial I told others to expect. I treat the fire as a clerical error in a life I assumed I had earned smoother. Peter's word lands on the preacher first: do not be surprised. You were told.

**Christ's suffering and the believer's**

And Peter keeps the suffering tethered to Christ, never floating free. The believer suffers as a Christian — under that name, sharing that pattern. "If anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name" (1 Peter 4:16). The suffering is not random pain. It is fellowship with the One who suffered first. So Peter ends with the steadiest instruction in the chapter. "Let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good" (1 Peter 4:19). Entrust. Hand the soul over. Christ did exactly this on the cross — into your hands I commit my spirit — and the armed exile does the same. You go on doing good, and you place your soul in the hands of a Creator who has never once been unfaithful.

Arm yourself for the fire.

Peter ends the letter by stooping. After five chapters on suffering and holiness and hope, he closes with a low, domestic word — about shepherds, and humility, and a worry you can hand to someone else. And he writes it with an old scar showing. He had once stood by a fire and denied his Lord three times, and the risen Christ had restored him with one repeated command: feed my sheep. Now Peter passes that command on. "Shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain, but eagerly" (1 Peter 5:2). He knows what it cost to be a shepherd who had failed. He does not write this from above the elders. He writes it as a fellow elder who knows the fire.

**Shepherds who do not own the flock**

Watch what Peter warns against, because it is the temptation of every leader. Compulsion — doing it because you are cornered, not because you love it. Shameful gain — using the flock as a revenue stream. And the deepest one: "not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock" (1 Peter 5:3). Domineering. Lording it over. The flock is God's, not the shepherd's, and the man who forgets that turns a calling into a small kingdom. Peter sets one motive over against all of it: "when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory" (1 Peter 5:4). There is a chief Shepherd, and every under-shepherd answers to him. You do not own the sheep. You watch them for the One who does, and who is coming back.

**Humility under the mighty hand**

Then Peter widens it from the elders to everyone. "Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you" (1 Peter 5:5-6). That phrase, clothe yourselves, may carry a memory. Peter had watched his Lord tie a towel around his waist and wash feet. He is telling the church to put on humility the way Christ put on that towel — to wear it, deliberately, as the working garment of the body.

And notice the hand. The mighty hand of God. The same hand that holds the exile under pressure is the hand that will lift him at the proper time. Humility is not pretending you are nothing. It is staying low under a hand strong enough to raise you when it chooses, and trusting its timing over your own.

**Cast it, because he cares**

Then comes the verse weary people have clung to for two thousand years. "Casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you" (1 Peter 5:7). Read it in context and it grows teeth. It is not a soft aside. It is grammatically tied to humbling yourself — casting your anxiety is how you humble yourself under that hand. Because pride hoards worry. Pride says the outcome depends on me, so I must carry it. Humility hands the weight to the One who actually governs the outcome. And the reason given is staggering in its plainness: because he cares for you. Not because he is obligated. Because he cares.

Let me say where I fail this, since the letter has implicated me at every turn. I preach the casting and practice the carrying. I lie awake holding what I told the congregation to hand over. The anxiety I keep is not strength. It is the pride of a man who has not yet stooped low enough to let go.

And Peter is sober about why the stakes are real. "Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith" (1 Peter 5:8-9). The casting of anxiety is not naive. There is a real enemy. But the exile resists him firm in faith, knowing the same sufferings are being met by the family of believers throughout the world.

**The God who restores**

And how does Peter leave them. With a promise built on the same pattern that has run through the whole letter — suffering first, then glory. "And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you" (1 Peter 5:10). He will himself do it. Not leave you to repair yourself. The God of all grace, who restored a fisherman by a fire, restores the exile after the little while of suffering — and the One through whom he calls and the One through whom he restores is Christ, into whose eternal glory the whole scattered, slandered, faithful family is going.

Stoop low. He lifts you.
